slides.title: Tokenization
slides.content: Tokenization • Text is encoded by a computer as a sequence of characters (string) • Words, spaces, and punctuation are encoded in the same way • We need to define and mark word boundaries: tokenization 2/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Tokenization

slides.title: Sentence detection
slides.content: Sentence detection • Certain punctuation characters are unambiguous (‘?’, ‘!’) • A dot (‘.’) is very ambiguous • Obama held his final address to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday. • Different genres such as the motet, the cantata, etc. developed throughout the centuries. • Context is important to determine where a sentence ends 5/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Language models
slides.content: Language models • Symbolic models (rule-based) give a hard, binary model of well-formed sentences • For many natural language processing tasks, a probabilistic model of a language (what is the probability of a string being well-formed?) is more useful • To specify a correct probability distribution, the probability of all sentences in a language must sum to 1 6/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Uses of language models
slides.content: Uses of language models • Speech recognition • ‘I ate a tomato’ is more likely than ‘eye eight atom eight oh’ • OCR & Handwriting recognition • More probable sentences are more likely correct readings • Machine translation • More likely sentences are probably better translations • Generation • More likely sentences are probably better natural language generations • Context sensitive spelling correction • ‘Their is a problem wit this sentence’ 7/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Completion prediction
slides.content: Completion prediction • Remember the guessing game of lecture 1: a language model predicts the next word in the sentence • Please turn off your mobile ____ • If he loses, he has only himself to ____ • Predictive text input systems can guess what you are typing and provide choices on how to complete it 8/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.content: Statistical language model • How to compute the probability of a sentence, e.g. the dog was running across the green field ? • We could count the number of times we attest the sentence, and divide by the total number of sentences in our corpus count(the dog was running across the green field) total number of sentences 9/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.content: Statistical language model How to compute p(the,dog,was,running,across,the,green,field) ? • We compute the joint probability by decomposing into conditional probabilities • p(the) →p(dog|the) →p(was|the dog) →p(running|the dog was) →p(across|the dog was running) →p(the|the dog was running across) →p(green|the dog was running across the) →p(field|the dog was running across the green) 10/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Estimating probabilities
slides.content: Estimating probabilities p(the) = count(the) count(∗) p(dog|the) = count(the,dog) count(the) p(green|across the) = count(across,the,green) count(across,the) 11/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: N-gram models
slides.content: N-gram models • Estimate probability of each word given prior context • Multiplication of individual probabilites gives sentence probability • An n-gram model uses only n–1 words of prior context • unigram: p(dog) • bigram: p(dog | the) • trigram: p(green | across the) • ... and so on • N-gram models are based on the Markov assumption • Future behavior of a dynamical system only depends on its recent history • In a kth-order Markov model, the next state only depends on the k most recent states • N-gram model is a (n–1)th-order Markov model. 12/46 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Part of speech
slides.content: Part of speech • Words can be categorised in classes that behave similarly 1 I can see a . 2 The is on the table. 3 She’s thinking about a . • Part of speech provides information about the context in the sentence • adjective often succeeded by noun • personal pronoun often succeeded by verb • Useful information for language processing applications • Automatically assigning part of speech: part of speech tagging 35/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sequence tagging
slides.content: Sequence tagging • Labeling a word in a sequence is the same as a simple classification • We have predicted labels for previous words • We use the predicted labels of previous words, as well as observed features (based on current, previous, and future words) in order to predict the best possible label for the current word crash in Stoke-on-Trent . NN IN NNP PUNCT O O ? ? Features w0 Stoke-on-Trent w−1 in w+1 . pos0 NNP pos−1 IN pos+1 PUNCT hasHyphen True label−1 O 39/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Global optimization
slides.content: Global optimization • Problem: we perform a series of local judgements, without taking into account the global optimality • We hope that the local conditions give us a global optimum • To solve our problem: • Instead of emitting a single answer, predict the n best answers • This way, we can compute the best global sequence 40/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Experiment
slides.content: Experiment • We have three sentiment classifiers • a list of hand-written rules (symbolic) • naive Bayes (statistical) • logistic regression (statistical) • Which one is better? how can we find out? • Common procedure in NLP: experiment 41/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Train, development, test
slides.content: Train, development, test training set dev test fit the model make choices report once • A model must be evaluated on data it has never seen: we care about generalization, not memorization • Training set: estimate the parameters (probabilities, weights) • Development (validation) set: for every choice you make (features, smoothing, thresholds, which model to keep: hyperparameters) • Test set: touched once, at the very end, for the number you report • Typical splits: 80/10/10 (train/dev/test) • Little data? Cross-validation on the training part; the test set still stays apart 42/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Leakage
slides.content: Leakage • Leakage: information about the test set finds its way into the model, so the reported score is too optimistic • It rarely looks like cheating: • you tried ten settings and kept the one that was best on the test set • the vocabulary was computed on all the data, before splitting • the same review (or a near-duplicate) occurs in both training and test • texts by the same author are included in both training and test • Everything that is learned or chosen must be learned or chosen without looking at the test set 43/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Baseline
slides.content: Baseline • ‘Our model reaches 95% accuracy’: is that good? • Example: toxic comment detection • about 95% of the comments are not toxic • A model that always answers not toxic scores 95%, while it does not find a single toxic comment • A number only means something next to a baseline • majority class (always predict the most frequent label) • a handful of simple rules, a word list • the simplest model that could possibly work • If your sophisticated model does not beat the simple baseline, you have a negative result 44/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Upper bound
slides.content: Upper bound • Opposite of the baseline: the best score that can be expected • Usually human performance: inter-annotator agreement • two annotators label the same items independently • percentage of agreement, or agreement corrected for chance (e.g. Krippendorff’s α) • The gold standard is only as reliable as the agreement between annotators • e.g. sentiment analysis: annotators often agree on 80–90% of the items • subjective tasks (irony, toxicity): considerably lower • A score is interpreted between baseline and upper bound 45/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Beyond accuracy
slides.content: Beyond accuracy Confusion matrix gold standard toxic not toxic system toxic true positive (TP) false positive (FP) not toxic false negative (FN) true negative (TN) P = TP TP + FP R = TP TP + FN F1 = 2PR P + R • The always-not toxic baseline: accuracy 95%, but recall and F1 for the class toxic: 0% 46/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Multiple classes
slides.content: Multiple classes • With more than two classes: compute P, R, F1 per class, then average • micro-average: pool all decisions →dominated by the frequent classes • macro-average: mean of the per-class scores →every class counts equally • With imbalanced classes, both averages can differ considerably 47/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Performance on sequences
slides.content: Performance on sequences • How to evaluate named entity recognition? • Precision, recall and F-measure, computed over entities rather than words • precision: percentage of entities returned by the system that are correct • recall: percentage of the entities in the test set that are found by the system • An entity is correct if both its boundaries and its type correspond to the test set • Charles Michel as PER, but only Michel tagged: incorrect • European Council tagged as LOC: incorrect • Per-word accuracy would be misleadingly high, as most words are labeled O 48/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Thresholds
slides.content: Thresholds • Naive Bayes and logistic regression output a probability • A decision requires a threshold, e.g. toxic if p > 0.5 • lower threshold: higher recall, lower precision • higher threshold: higher precision, lower recall • The threshold is a hyperparameter: it is set on the development set recall precision p > 0.9 p > 0.5 p > 0.1 49/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Significance
slides.content: Significance • Example: naive Bayes 84.2% accuracy, logistic regression 84.7% accuracy • Is logistic regression better? Not necessarily • the test set is a sample: a different set of 1,000 reviews yields a different score • models with random components (initialization, order of the data) yield different results with different random seeds • Guidelines: • use a sufficiently large test set; report size • repeat with different seeds or folds; report mean and standard deviation • small differences between models are often not significant: use a significance test (e.g. McNemar’s test, paired bootstrap) 50/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Error analysis
slides.content: Error analysis • An evaluation score indicates how often a model makes mistakes, not why • Error analysis: inspection of the errors on the development set • take a sample of errors (e.g. 50) and categorize them • which categories are frequent, and which could be addressed? • Linguistic knowledge is often helpful • Goal: explain a pattern of errors 51/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Checklist
slides.content: Checklist 1 Keep a separate test set, and use it only once 2 Avoid leakage 3 Compare against a baseline 4 Choose metrics that suit the task and the class distribution 5 Make all choices (incl. thresholds) on the development set 6 Report the uncertainty of the results 7 Analyze the errors 8 Support every claim with results 52/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
